The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $\mu_0$ is a premeasure on an algebra $\mathcal A_0$ of subsets of $X$ and $\mu^*$ is its induced outer set function, then $\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal M_{\mu^*}$ and $\mu^*|_{\mathcal A_0}=\mu_0$. The restriction of $\mu^*$ to $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$ is therefore a measure extending $\mu_0$.

Equivalently: assuming countable choice, the induced outer measure restricts to a complete measure on its Carathéodory sigma-algebra and to a measure on $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$ extending $\mu_0$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

From any sequence in $X$, retain an infinite subsequence constant at $i_1$, then a further infinite subsequence constant at $i_2$, and so on; taking the diagonal subsequence makes each fixed coordinate eventually constant. For $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K$ with $2^{-K}<\varepsilon$. Two sufficiently late diagonal terms agree at the first $K$ sites, so their metric distance is at most $2^{-K}<\varepsilon$ and they converge to the coordinatewise limit.

A cylinder depends on finitely many coordinates. For any two cylinder presentations of the same set, pass to the union of their finite coordinate sets and use consistency of the finite-dimensional probabilities; this proves that the induced weight on the cylinder algebra is well-defined. The same finite-coordinate representation proves finite additivity and normalization.

Enumerate the countable cylinders as $C_1,C_2,\ldots$. By [F3], choose a subsequence on which the probabilities of $C_1$ converge; successively choose nested subsequences for $C_2,C_3,\ldots$, then take the diagonal subsequence. Countable Choice justifies this countable sequence of subsequence selections. The limits are normalized and consistent on every finite coordinate set.

To prove compactness directly, suppose an open cover has no finite subcover. Starting with $X$, successively split the current cylinder by the next coordinate into finitely many subcylinders; at least one remains without a finite subcover, and choose the first such cylinder in the fixed alphabet order. The resulting nested cylinders determine one configuration $\sigma$. Some cover member contains $\sigma$ and, being open, contains a basic cylinder fixing finitely many coordinates of $\sigma$. A sufficiently late nested cylinder is contained in that member, contradicting its selection. Thus every open cover has a finite subcover. The cylinders form a countable clopen basis, so they generate exactly the Borel sigma-algebra.

If a cylinder $C$ is a disjoint union of countably many cylinders $C_n$, compactness of $C$ gives a finite subcover from the open cover $(C_n)$. Disjointness forces every other $C_n$ to be empty, so finite additivity gives countable additivity whenever the union is in $\mathcal C$; the cylinder weight is therefore a premeasure. Apply [F1] to extend it under the stated Countable Choice assumption. The cylinder family is a pi-system generating $\sigma(\mathcal C)$, so [F2] gives uniqueness.

The extension in step 3.1 gives a probability measure with those cylinder values. Local functions are finite linear combinations of cylinder indicators. Every continuous $f$ is uniformly approximated by local functions. If uniform continuity failed, there would be pairs agreeing on successively longer initial coordinate sets while their $f$-values stayed separated by some $\varepsilon>0$; compactness gives convergent subsequences of both sequences to the same configuration, contradicting continuity. Thus for large $K$, fixing the coordinates after the first $K$ to any fixed reference tail gives a local approximation with uniform error at most $\varepsilon$. Cylinder convergence therefore gives convergence of integrals first for local functions and then for every continuous $f$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For probability vectors $p,q$ on a finite set $A$, there is a coupling $(X,Y)$ with $\Pr(X\ne Y)=\tfrac12\sum_{a\in A}|p(a)-q(a)|$. For a finite region $\Lambda$ with strictly positive single-site Gibbs conditionals, the random-scan heat-bath chain has the finite-volume Gibbs law as its unique stationary distribution. This chain is an auxiliary finite-state proof device, not a physical time evolution.

Assume Countable Choice, a finite nonempty alphabet $A$, and a proper consistent finite-range specification $\gamma$ on $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$, with finite range as defined in [[def-csm-lattice-gibbs-specification]]. No translation invariance is required. For every exhaustion $\Lambda_n\uparrow\mathbb Z^d$ and every sequence of exterior configurations $\eta_n$, the measures $\gamma_{\Lambda_n}(\cdot\mid\eta_n)$ extended with the fixed exterior have a cylinder-convergent subsequence. Every such subsequential limit is a DLR state. Consequently the DLR state set is nonempty, convex, and closed under cylinder convergence. No uniqueness is asserted.

Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$ and a finite nonempty alphabet $A$. A configuration is a function $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to A$. An interaction list consists of a finite index set $\mathcal R$ and, for each $r\in\mathcal R$, a finite nonempty shape $S_r\subset\mathbb Z^d$ containing $0$ and a function $\Phi_r:A^{S_r}\to\mathbb R$. The index $r$ is part of the data: two equal shapes with different indices represent two terms and are both counted. Every translate $x+S_r$ contributes once, with value $\Phi_r((\sigma_{x+y})_{y\in S_r})$.

The range is $R=\max_{r\in\mathcal R}\operatorname{diam}_\infty(S_r)$, with $R=0$ when $\mathcal R$ is empty. For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, define the free-volume energy and the energy conditioned on an exterior configuration $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$ by
$$H^{\mathrm{free}}_\Lambda(\sigma)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\ \sum_{x:x+S_r\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi_r(\sigma_{x+S_r}),\qquad E_\Lambda(\tau_\Lambda\mid\eta)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\ \sum_{x:(x+S_r)\cap\Lambda\ne\varnothing}\Phi_r((\tau_\Lambda\eta)_{x+S_r}).$$
These are finite sums: for each finite shape $S_r$, only finitely many anchors $x$ make $x+S_r$ meet $\Lambda$. Terms meeting $\Lambda$ but not contained in it appear in the conditional energy and not in the free-volume energy. The definitions are mathematical and assign no physical units; a physical model must state its units separately.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$ and a finite nonempty alphabet $A$. A configuration is a function $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to A$. An interaction list consists of a finite index set $\mathcal R$ and, for each $r\in\mathcal R$, a finite nonempty shape $S_r\subset\mathbb Z^d$ containing $0$ and a function $\Phi_r:A^{S_r}\to\mathbb R$. The index $r$ is part of the data: two equal shapes with different indices represent two terms and are both counted. Every translate $x+S_r$ contributes once, with value $\Phi_r((\sigma_{x+y})_{y\in S_r})$.

The range is $R=\max_{r\in\mathcal R}\operatorname{diam}_\infty(S_r)$, with $R=0$ when $\mathcal R$ is empty. For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$, define the free-volume energy and the energy conditioned on an exterior configuration $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$ by
$$H^{\mathrm{free}}_\Lambda(\sigma)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\ \sum_{x:x+S_r\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi_r(\sigma_{x+S_r}),\qquad E_\Lambda(\tau_\Lambda\mid\eta)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\ \sum_{x:(x+S_r)\cap\Lambda\ne\varnothing}\Phi_r((\tau_\Lambda\eta)_{x+S_r}).$$
These are finite sums: for each finite shape $S_r$, only finitely many anchors $x$ make $x+S_r$ meet $\Lambda$. Terms meeting $\Lambda$ but not contained in it appear in the conditional energy and not in the free-volume energy. The definitions are mathematical and assign no physical units; a physical model must state its units separately.

derivations.claim: Around each dual vertex the product of the four primal nearest-neighbor spin products is $1$, since each corner spin occurs twice. Hence the number of disagreeing bonds incident to that vertex is even. The mismatch graph is finite because all spins outside the finite box are $+1$.

Start from an unused edge and extend a trail along unused edges. Since every vertex has even degree, the trail cannot stop at a vertex other than its starting vertex; finiteness therefore gives a closed trail. Taking the segment between the first repeated vertex extracts a simple cycle. Removing its edges preserves even degree at every vertex, so repeating the finite procedure decomposes every edge into edge-disjoint cycles. The square lattice has no loops, parallel edges, or triangles, so each cycle has length at least four.

Dual vertices have half-integer coordinates, so a ray from an integer-height primal site meets no dual vertex. For horizontally adjacent sites, the symmetric difference of their rightward rays is exactly the horizontal unit segment crossing their joining primal bond, so their parity differs exactly when that bond is crossed by $\gamma$. For vertically adjacent sites, truncate both rays at a vertical line beyond the finite cycle; the boundary of the resulting finite strip is a closed curve. A closed polygonal cycle meets this boundary an even number of times modulo two, and the far side has no intersections, so the parity difference is exactly the crossing of the vertical bond between the two rays.

Every primal site outside a rectangle containing $\gamma$ has parity zero, since its ray either misses $\gamma$ or crosses the full cycle an even number of times; thus the inside is finite. In a plus-boundary box, any site outside the box has an outward lattice path to infinity lying entirely in the plus exterior. Along this path no bond is a mismatch, so step 3.1 keeps its parity zero; hence every cycle-inside site lies in the box. Along any primal path, the spin changes exactly on mismatch edges. A path from the origin to the all-plus exterior therefore crosses an odd number of mismatch edges if $s_0=-1$. For each cycle in the edge-disjoint decomposition from step 2.1, step 3.1 says its parity changes along the path exactly when that path crosses one of its edges; its parity is zero at the exterior endpoint. The sum modulo two of the cycle parity changes is the total mismatch-edge count, which is odd, so at least one cycle has origin parity one, as claimed.
